examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $E_1$ and $E_2$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find $E_2^{-1}.$ We write down $E_2$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14058013/assets/a8c0d76a5f06d1077eb45b6af4761434164602747f54d9644646b654d319b373.png)

Now, we can find the product $E_1 E_{2}^{-1}\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14058013/assets/f16a0b0e573cf3a8022f9c62993364a0d708c3a0cff0b4bb4cb0eadde7848f56.png)

feedback.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -10 & 1\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
We write down $B$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[B\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -10 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+10{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 10 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{B}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
